19846-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The eleventh edition of Encyclopaedia Britannica is often called the finest ever made. This volume runs from Bulgaria to Calgary. Its Bulgaria article describes the Malka Planina and Ikhtiman hills near Sofia. The Balkan range appears as a continuation of the great Alpine system. Pine-clad steeps there recall the Alps more than the lowlands. Scholarly articles fill the volume at that density.

Published in 1910 and 1911, the eleventh edition enlisted top scholars. Its long signed articles still get consulted today. A single volume holds geography, biography, and science in alphabetical march. Bulgaria to Calgary spans empires and a young Canadian city. The edition marks print reference at its peak. Libraries kept it in daily use for decades.
20444-the-knickerbocker-or-new-york-mont:
The Knickerbocker was one of America's leading monthly magazines, and this is its March 1844 issue. Its pages mix essays, tales, poems, and reviews for a growing reading public. The magazine took its name from Washington Irving's comic history of New York.

One essay takes up the new philosophy of the transcendentalists. The writer argues that all thinking men find themselves forced to be transcendentalists, whether they know themselves by that name or not. A skeptic answers with a flat Poh. The exchange shows the magazine's lively mix of ideas and wit in the young republic.
20845-the-knickerbocker-or-new-york-mont:
Marathon and Iona stir less fire, argues The Knickerbocker for April 1844, than fields hallowed by Hampden or Falkland. Johnson's stately phrase on patriotism gets a tart reply here. English blood and English faith, the piece insists, move English hearts most.

The Knickerbocker, a New York monthly, mixed tales, essays, verse, and reviews. It gave early print to many American writers of note. Volume twenty-three's April number froze one month of that rich mix. Readers can sample the tone of American letters in the 1840s, confident, bookish, and keen to prove its worth.
6202-when-valmond-came-to-pontiac-the-st:
When Valmond Came to Pontiac, volume one, stands by itself in Parker's work, like nothing else he wrote, and might be called an historical fantasy. It followed The Trail of the Sword, preceded The Seats of the Mighty, and appeared in summer 1895 to an extremely gratifying critical reception.

Critics, Parker felt, realized what he tried to do, a great deal in itself. One journal said it read as written at a sitting, another called it a tour de force, and the grave Athenaeum praised it in a key likely to make him nervous.
6203-when-valmond-came-to-pontiac-the-st:
Valmond in the second volume plays his part with equal aplomb, prince or plebeian, at Elise Malboir's simple home and at Manoir Hilaire, where Madame Chalice receives him. His dress holds nothing bizarre: black long coat, silk stockings, waistcoat collar faced with white, full white neckerchief, and enamelled shoes with silver buckles.

His present repose and decorum contrast strangely with fanciful display at first introduction. Madame Chalice approves instantly, finding the costume, though a generation out of time, sedately refined and in the picture. She welcomes him where Frontenac, Vaudreuil, and Sir Guy Carleton were entertained.
6204-when-valmond-came-to-pontiac-the-st:
Valmond's sickness opens the third volume of When Valmond Came to Pontiac, coming like a whirlwind, leaving the question what will remain when it passes. The fight goes on in quiet hills: a man of no great stature or strength against a monster racking him in fierce embrace.

A thousand scenes flash through Valmond's brain while the great wheel of torture turns, breaking and mending him again upon it. Spinning like a tireless moth through fiery air, he cries in vain to the wheelman to stop, while stars blink and wind whips clouds past.
9580-anti-slavery-poems-and-songs-of-lab:
Volume three of Whittier's complete works pairs his anti-slavery poems with his songs of labor and reform. Anti-slavery verse runs from To William Lloyd Garrison and Toussaint L'Ouverture to The Slave-Ships, The Hunters of Men, and a Virginia slave mother's farewell. Labor songs praise toil, skill, and the dignity of working folk. Whittier wrote both groups as a Quaker reformer, not a mere singer.

Later poems take in Texas, Faneuil Hall, and the branded hand, then turn to war-time verse and emancipation hymns. The whole volume reads as a life of conscience in verse. A reader gets Whittier the reformer at full stretch, with poems that helped move a nation toward freedom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andres-cavo:
Frequently quoted on Spanish-Mexican history, Andres Cavo was born at Guadalajara in Mexico on 21 January 1729. He joined the Society of Jesus on 14 January 1758. After the order's expulsion from Mexico in 1767, he went to Italy with its other members.

For Mexico City's municipality he wrote an important chronicle covering events from the conquest of Mexico in 1521 to 1767. Bustamante holds that it was composed after his expatriation, while Cavo was at Rome. Out of delicacy, Cavo stopped the work once his order had been expelled from Mexico. He preserved and co-ordinated a large number of facts found nowhere else. Bustamante edited and continued the chronicle to 1836, but without Cavo's impartiality. The book, Los Tres Siglos en Mexico, was published at Jalapa in Mexico in 1870.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aquino-sora-a:
Aquino, Sora, and Pontecorvo form an Italian diocese directly subject to the Holy See, covering twenty-nine towns in Caserta province and seven in Aquila. Aquino became a see in 465, Sora in 275, bearing a regular bishops' list from 1221, and Pontecorvo on 28 June 1725, at once united to Aquino. Sora joined them in 1818 under Pius VII, and the bishop's seat stands at Rocca Secca.

Figures in the article give Aquino 50,150 people, twenty-one parishes, and ninety-one churches and chapels. Sora has 95,200 people, forty-four parishes, and 220 churches or chapels. Pontecorvo counts 12,000 people, eight parishes, and twenty-five churches or chapels. St. Constans, bishop of Aquino in 566, is cathedral patron, and the towns claim Juvenal the poet, Emperor Pescennius Niger, and Thomas Aquinas among their sons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belgrade-and-:
Belgrade and Smederevo form a single entry on two linked sees, or bishoprics, in Serbia, in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. The piece follows their tangled past from an ancient Roman town through Slav invasions, Hungarian and Venetian claims, and later Serbian rule. It treats the sees as united, with a history marked by moves, losses, and rebuilding.

Belgrade appears first as Singidunum, an early bishopric that faded under invasion, then revived in medieval times with bishops named from 1059 onward. Smederevo enters as a neighbouring seat tied to the same shifting frontier. The entry stresses how thin Catholic life had become there by its own day, with a scattered flock served under hard conditions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-bra:
Francisco Bravo, a doctor from Osuna in Spain, is known as writer of the first medicine book printed in America. His Opera Medicinalia was published at Mexico in 1570. Three years earlier, Pedrarias de Benavides had published his Secrets of Surgery at Valladolid in Spain, a work invaluable for Indian medicinal practices and the earliest on those topics known. Bravo's book holds the honour of being the first medical treatise printed on American soil.

Little else is known of Bravo: he began practice at Seville in 1553, reached Mexico between then and 1570, and his date and place of death are unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-radulph-of-ri:
Radulph of Rivo was a historian and liturgist. This encyclopedia entry places his birth at Breda, in Dutch Brabant, about the middle of the fourteenth century, and his death at Tongres on 3 November 1403. He studied across Europe: in Italy, where he stood in 1362, at Paris, and at Orléans from 1367 to 1375, learning canon and civil law. He was subdeacon by 1371 at the latest.

The deanery of Tongres came to him in 1371, though he took up the charge only in 1383. Between those years he returned to Italy, and in 1381 he still stood at Rome, where Simon of Constantinople, Archbishop of Thebes, taught him Greek. After 1390 a vice-dean replaced him at Tongres. He then joined the new University of Cologne, founded in 1388, and served as its rector in 1397. His works on church offices, the last two unpublished, close an entry drawn from Balau, Batiffol and Mohlberg.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastiano-de:
Sebastiano de Herrera Barnuevo, painter, architect, sculptor, and etcher, was born at Madrid in 1611 or 1619 and died there in 1671. Son of Antonio Herrera, a sculptor of fair ability, he learned the rudiments from his father and was then placed with Cano. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a court artist in Philip IV's Madrid.

Under Cano he advanced so fast in painting and sculpture that Philip IV took him into service. The king set him to adorn the Atocha chapel of Our Lady and named him keeper of the Escorial, where he worked thereafter. Most of his pictures remain in Madrid. His masterpiece, St Barnabas in the Escorial council chamber, long passed as Guido's work. Nearly as famous are his Beatification of St Augustine and his Nativity, with colouring as brilliant as Titian's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-serajevo-sara:
Sarajevo's church history, as told in this entry, was blighted first by Arianism and the wanderings of peoples, then irreparably by the Eastern Schism. To this day, the entry says, forty-three per cent of the population are Greek Orthodox, calling themselves Servians. From earliest times the Church opposed the Bogomiles, a Manichaean offshoot known under many names, from Paulicians to Marcionites, whose many graves prove their numbers in Bosnia.

Franciscans worked with the secular clergy from 1292 onward. When the last native king, Stephan Tomasevic, was seized and beheaded by the Turks in 1463, many Catholics renounced the faith to save their property and became Mohammedans now called Begs. Nearly all Bogomiles did the same. The few who stayed true sank to rayahs, serfs without civil rights, and the Church endured four centuries of hardship, losing property and seeing its faithful migrate.
govdocs-archive_org-Village-Voice-Pike-R:
The Pike Committee was the House of Representatives' 1970s investigation into American intelligence agencies, the House counterpart to the Senate's Church Committee. Its final report was never officially released, but the Village Voice published it in 1976 after it was leaked.

The reprint carries the committee's findings on the CIA and other agencies: covert operations, domestic abuses, and failures of oversight. The leak itself became a press-freedom fight, since Congress had voted to keep the report secret. The file was declassified for release in 2012, letting readers see the document Washington once tried to suppress.
library-of-the-world-s-best-literature-a:
Charles Dudley Warner edited this first volume of a large anthology of world writing. Associate editors Hamilton Wright Mabie, Lucia Gilbert Runkle, and George Henry Warner helped him. A council of university professors from Harvard, Yale, Princeton, and other schools advised the project. The set aimed to gather the best literature, ancient and modern, in one place.

Each volume presents chosen works and passages from many authors and periods. Readers can move from old classics to newer writing without hunting down rare books. The Connoisseur Edition format shows the set was made for home libraries. For modern readers, the volume also shows what educated Americans around 1896 counted as essential reading. Yale's Thomas Lounsbury and Michigan's president James Angell sat on that council. Columbia's Brander Matthews, a professor of literature, served alongside them.
podcast-dannyjones-viUguxehZVo:
Anesthesiologist Stuart Hameroff joins Danny Jones to talk about proof of a soul, a vast NASA-linked study, and awareness at death. Hameroff is known for a theory that links the mind to quantum acts in the brain's small tubes.

Hameroff lays out his case that the mind is not just the brain at work. He talks about what may occur at the edge of death and what the big study found. Jones asks how his peers treat the theory. Listeners get a deep talk on the soul from a man of science. The library holds it as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-gLJowTOkZVo:
Neuroscientist Andrew Huberman joins Joe Rogan for episode 1513 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Huberman, a Stanford professor, became famous for his Huberman Lab podcast and its practical health protocols. This visit distills his system into a single long talk.

Huberman explains how sleep, morning sunlight, and temperature shape focus and mood each day. He gives simple, free habits backed by lab research that listeners can start at once. Rogan shares his own routines and asks how to fix broken sleep. The health-minded get one of the show's most useful hours, full of steps that cost nothing.
podcast-tuckercarlson-5TT3o9SzIvo:
Jimmy Dore, the comedian and political commentator, joins Tucker Carlson to discuss the murder of Charlie Kirk. They also discuss Congressman Thomas Massie. Dore then traces his own path to faith through what he calls a propaganda hellscape, a media environment he believes lies as a matter of routine.

Dore comes from the left and Carlson from the right, and their agreement on media distrust is the episode's engine. Kirk's killing is treated as a national turning point, Massie as a rare honest man in Congress. The faith thread surprises listeners who know Dore's older work. The recording captures a cross-ideological alliance in formation, two populists comparing notes on power, violence, and God, and finding more shared ground than either expected.
podcast-tuckercarlson-gG-e06kJTvo:
A state-sponsored death cult disguised as healthcare is Tucker Carlson's charge in this grim episode. Carlson argues that government-backed medicine has turned toward ending life rather than saving it. He says the system preys most on white patients and the weak, who have the least power to resist.

The episode lays out the policies and cases Carlson reads as proof of the pattern. He asks why assisted death expands while care and hope shrink. His indictment treats the trend as a moral collapse, not a budget choice. Alarmed and grieving viewers get the host's darkest view of the medical state.
the-trained-memory-being-the-fourth-of-a: Warren Hilton's Trained Memory, issued in 1920 under the Literary Digest for the Society of Applied Psychology, is the fourth of twelve volumes applying psychology to personal and business efficiency. This record gives its title page and the start of a contents list. Chapter one names four memory processes; chapter two promises the mental treasure vault and its lost combination, causes of forgetfulness, waxen tablets, and the flash of inspiration. Hilton's system is outlined in these headings, while his lessons begin beyond them.
when-valmond-came-to-pontiac-the-story-o:
Volume one of Gilbert Parker's When Valmond Came to Pontiac carries the same introduction as the complete record. Parker calls the book a historical fantasy unlike his other work. It appeared in the summer of 1895 and won strong praise. One journal said it read as though written at a sitting, and Parker grants the point.

The draft, he says, was done in four weeks of work by night and day. He would rise at two or three in the morning to write till breakfast. The tale brings Valmond, who claims a link to Napoleon, into the village of Pontiac in Quebec. Old French loyalties wake at his coming. Parker wrote as if possessed, and the tale keeps that heat.
